title: Prevalence and associated factors of undernutrition among adolescents in India: a systematic review
abstract: BackgroundUndernutrition is a major public health challenge among Indian adolescents in India where 253 million of them are in the age group of 10–19 years. In spite of several intensive efforts through various program interventions and care, research studies find a less encouraging improvement in nutritional scenarios. The present systematic review aimed to determine the pooled prevalence and associated factors of undernutrition (stunting and underweight) among Indian adolescents.MethodsWe searched e-databases of MEDLINE/PubMed, EMBASE, Google Scholar, and Cochrane library for the period between the years 2000 and 2021. The peer-reviewed and empirical studies analyzing the prevalence of undernutrition among Indian adolescents and its associated factors were eligible for inclusion. The quality of the study reports included in the review was evaluated using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale. The random-effect model with the Dersimonian and Laird method, at 95% confidence intervals, was used for estimating the overall effect. Subgroup analysis was conducted to investigate the possible sources of heterogeneity. Publication bias was assessed through visual examination of funnel plots and objectively by Egger’s regression test.ResultsA total of forty eligible studies with a pooled sample size of 67,865 adolescents were included to determine the prevalence of undernutrition among adolescents in India. The pooled prevalence of stunting and underweight in India was 41.1% (95% CI: 35.9, 46.0) and 32.6% (95% CI: 26.8, 37.1) respectively. It was also found that the rate of stunting prevalence was high among late adolescents and underweight was high among early adolescents. Age, gender, income, family size, caste, parental education, and occupation were the significant associated factors of the prevalence of stunting and underweight among adolescents in India.ConclusionThe prevalence of stunting and underweight among adolescents is still a high concern in India. The results of this review posit the need of an integrated effort to reduce undernutrition in India and identify research priorities in this field.Supplementary InformationThe online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12889-025-22054-2.

sections.title: Body
sections.text:
Undernutrition is a widespread and major public health challenge in India causing high morbidity and mortality by deteriorating the quality of life [–]. The outcomes of various efforts towards reduction of undernutrition in India have not been very encouraging, despite various program and policy level reforms and interventions []. Undernutrition continues to remain a concern among children and adolescents in both rural and urban areas [–]. The latest National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5), India, 2019-21 has reported a high prevalence of undernutrition among children under five years (27.3%, underweight; 30.1%, stunted; 18.5%, wasted) []. However, there is a major gap in similar nationally representative surveys exclusively reporting the nutritional status among Indian adolescents ranging from 10–19 years. On the other hand, many individual large-scale studies highlighted the high prevalence of undernutrition among adolescent boys and girls in India. In 2018, a study on teenage girls (13–19 years) across 30 states reported that every second adolescent girl is underweight and anaemic []. In the Comprehensive National Nutritional Survey (CNNS), 2019, the prevalence of stunting and underweight among adolescents was 26.4% and 24% respectively [].

Considering India’s population in Census 2011, the adolescent population (10–19 years age group) in the country is 253 million which constitutes about one-fifth of the World’s total adolescent population and a substantial section in Asia also []. So, the health of adolescents in India defines the health of adolescents in regional and global scenarios. Here, it is important to mention that the adolescent period is a significant phase during the life course of an individual. It is a major transitional period while attaining adulthood. It expounds on changes around social, biological, and psychological development and is permeated by remarkable rapid development []. Inadequate nutrition severely affects the immediate physical, psychological, and cognitive growth of adolescents along with affecting their development in the long run.

Evidence shows that there is a major gap in nationally representative surveys and data on adolescents. National Family Health Survey does not collect data on the adolescent age group exclusively. On the other hand, the majority of nutritional interventions, as well as research on undernutrition in India at national to various local levels, have primarily concentrated on preschool children and those below five years []. So, overall, there is a paucity of national survey-based evidence as well as targeted intervention around the nutritional health of adolescents in India, across communities. Our formative research, however, found that there are a number of studies in India evaluating adolescent undernutrition and its related risk factors.

So, to understand all the scenarios and various prevailing concerns, there was a strong need for a detailed and comprehensive evidence-based review and evaluation of available literature on adolescent undernutrition in India; the present systematic review aimed to address this objective by providing a panoramic view of undernutrition among them. Our formative research also finds that in spite of several studies evaluating adolescent undernutrition in India and its related risk factors, no systematic review has been undertaken. Therefore, this systematic review was planned, to fill this gap. The findings of the study will also have a strong policy perspective by providing details status for the further decision-making process. The main objectives of this review are; 1) To determine the pooled prevalence of undernutrition (stunting and underweight) among Indian adolescents aged 10 to 19 years; 2) To identify the associated risk factors of undernutrition among adolescents in India.

sections.title: Methods
sections.text:
The protocol of the present systematic review is available elsewhere []. The protocol of this review was registered at the International Prospective Register of Systematic Review and Meta-analysis (PROSPERO: CRD42021286814). This review was prepared according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-analyses guidelines []. The PRISMA- 2020 checklist is given in the supplementary material (Additional File 1) in the Supporting Information. The data sources, study design, search strategy, and inclusion and exclusion criteria have already been discussed in the protocol.

For this review, studies published between the years 2000 and 2021 in the PubMed/MEDLINE, EMBASE, Google Scholar, and Cochrane databases were systematically searched. The articles were searched separately by using the following key terms: “adolescents” OR “teenagers” OR “young youths” AND “undernutrition” OR “nutritional deficiency” OR micronutrient deficiency” OR “nutritional status” OR “underweight” OR “Stunting” OR “wasting” AND “India”. The search strategy is provided in Additional File 2. Also, the reference lists of the included articles were also searched to find out the eligible articles. The search process for relevant articles was undertaken during the period of September 2000 to October 2021. The criteria for this time period was decided based on years with major reporting period and relevance of studies. The screening and selection process was conducted through different inclusion and exclusion criteria. We included studies that reported: 1) Indian adolescents between the age group of 10–19 years; 2) WHO growth standards; 3) anthropometric indicators such as stunting and underweight; 4) all observational studies (cross-sectional, cohort, case–control studies indicating the prevalence of undernutrition among adolescents). Studies were excluded that reported: 1) Children under ten years, adult population and married pregnant adolescents; 2) Studies reporting micronutrient deficiency exclusively; 3) Studies reporting anaemia exclusively or diseases causing growth retardation like HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis among adolescents; 4) the paper published other than in English language; 5) studies with small sample size (< 100). We excluded all the articles, such as editorials, review articles, and case reports, without original data.

Two reviewers (J.P. and B.S.B.) collected all the relevant articles and removed the duplicates. The published articles adhering to the search criteria in the titles, keywords, and abstracts were included in the next step. The full-text articles were then assessed independently by the reviewers. The criteria for the PICOS/PECOS (Participants, Interventions/exposures, Comparators, Outcomes, and Study designs) were followed to identify the eligible articles (Table 1). During this process, if the full text of the study was not available, the reviewers contacted the author to provide the full text. Nevertheless, if the authors did not respond or provide the full text after two-mail contacts, then the article was excluded from the review because of the inability to assess the quality of articles in the absence of full text. All the selected articles approved by both reviewers were included in the study. In the context of any discrepancy among the reviewers, it was resolved through discussion and mutual consent, or in consultation with third reviewer (S. K. A.). Table 1PICOS criteria for inclusion of studiesParameterDescriptionParticipants (P)Adolescents between the age group of 10–19 yearsInterventions/Exposures (I)Determinants of undernutrition: the determinants are the exposures that increase the prevalence of undernutrition among adolescents. These risk factors are the educational and occupational status of parents, household income, age, sex, food security, and dietary habitsComparators (C)The reference group of each determinant in each study. the prevalence of undernutrition (stunting and underweight) in rural and urban areas, the prevalence of undernutrition among boys and girls, and nutritional status among early and late adolescentsOutcomes (O)The prevalence of undernutrition (stunting and underweight) and its associated factors or determinants among Indian adolescentsStudy designs (S)All observational studies (cross-sectional, cohort, and case–control studies) indicating the prevalence of undernutrition among adolescents

PICOS criteria for inclusion of studies

Both the reviewers (J. P. and B.S.B.) independently extracted the relevant data from the eligible articles after the screening of full-text articles. The extracted data were presented in a predefined and standardized data extraction format on a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet. The relevant data included the name of the author/s, year of publication, study design, place of the study, region of the study, sample size, the age range of study participants, sex of study participants, population characteristics, the prevalence of stunting, and prevalence of underweight.

The quality of included studies was assessed by adopting the Newcastle–Ottawa Quality Assessment Scale (NOS) for cross-sectional, case–control, and cohort studies by the reviewers (J.P., B.S.B and P.K.P.) independently []. The parameters used for quality assessment were representativeness of the sample (Sample strategy), age, sample size, cut-offs, and reference measure for adolescent undernutrition status. The final scoring system was comprised of 10-point criteria for rating the quality elements of each study. This assessment scale was used to assess the internal and external validity, risk of bias, and methodological quality of each included study (cross-sectional, cohort, and case–control studies). The quality assessment tool has 3 parts. The first part deals with the methodological quality of each original study such as objectives, sample size, and sampling technique with a gradation scale of 1 to 5 stars. The second part of the tool considers the comparability of studies and is graded out of 2 stars. The third part of the tool considers the outcome measures and data analysis and is graded on 3 stars. Studies scoring a total of > 6 stars out of 10 were included in the systematic review (Additional File 3). Quality assessment was checked independently by four authors, and any disagreements were resolved by discussion and mutual consensus. If the discrepancy still persisted, the average scores of the reviewers were taken into consideration. Similarly, in the case of determinants, each determinant or factor with the outcome variables was critically assessed. Similar cut-off points were employed for all prevalence studies of undernutrition. The level of risk of bias in each of the parameters was presented separately for each study.

The present systematic review was conducted using STATA version 17.0 (StataCorp. 2021. Stata Statistical Software: Release 17. College Station, TX: StataCorp LLC). The extracted data from each study using a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet were imported to STATA data file format. Undernutrition-specific estimates for stunting and underweight were pooled separately using a random-effects model weighted by the inverse of the variance. The random-effect model with the Dersimonian and Laird (DL) method, at 95% confidence intervals, was used for estimating the overall effect [, ].

The existence of heterogeneity among studies was assessed by Higgins’s I2 test statistics []. The heterogeneity of the studies was classified as low, moderate, and high based on the I2 value as less than 25%, 50%, and 75%, respectively. Results were considered to be statistically significant only if the p-value was less than or equal to 0.05. Subgroup analysis was performed in order to determine the possible sources of heterogeneity in the study characteristics. Subgroup analysis was conducted by year of publication (2005–15 & 2016–2021), gender (male vs female), age (early vs late adolescence), place of study (rural vs urban vs tribal), and regions (East, West, North, South, North-East and Central) to investigate the potential sources of heterogeneity between subgroups. The presence of publication bias was conducted to assess the risk of bias across studies through visual examination of funnel plots and statistical support of confirmatory and/or objectivity testing with Egger and Begg’s linear regression test at a 5% level of significance. [, ] Leave-one-out and cumulative meta-analyses were performed as additional sensitivity analyses. A leave-one-out sensitivity analysis was also done to confirm the consistency of estimates by dropping each study at a time. The cumulative meta-analysis was performed by accumulating studies one at a time, ordered chronologically, to examine the trends in the pooled estimate.

sections.title: Results
sections.text:
First, a total of 1,890 studies were identified reporting the prevalence of undernutrition among Indian adolescents and its associated factors; this was done by referring to four electronic databases along with references from key articles. Out of these searched studies, 181 studies were excluded based on duplication; 1599 were excluded by title and abstract screening. The remaining 110 full texts of studies were assessed for eligibility. Of those, 70 records were further excluded based on selection criteria: 1) absence of stunting and underweight prevalence in the study; 2) incomplete information; 3) studies other than community-based; 4) non-segregated or poorly defined age group and difficult to extract data for adolescents. Finally, 40 studies were selected for systematic review after the quality check (Supplementary file) [, –, –]. The procedures of screening and selection of these forty eligible studies were presented in a PRISMA flow diagram (Fig. 1).Fig. 1PRISMA Flow diagram of the studies included in the review of adolescent undernutrition in India

PRISMA Flow diagram of the studies included in the review of adolescent undernutrition in India

The characteristics of the selected studies were summarised and presented in Table 2. All forty studies were cross-sectional studies published between 2000 and 2021. There were two studies published between the period of 2000 and 2010 [, ], while the other thirty-eight studies were published during the period of 2011 and later. A total of 67,865 adolescents from the selected studies were included in this review and showed a sample size ranging from a minimum of 135 [] to a maximum of 20,597 []. Of the forty studies, nineteen studies [, , , , , , –, , , , , , , , ] were included to estimate the pooled prevalence of stunting along with thirty-eight studies [, –, –, –, –] for the underweight in this review. The selected studies were divided based on six major regional distributions such as East, West, North, South, North-East and Central India as per the study’s geographical location. Eleven studies were from Eastern India, including the states like Bihar, Jharkhand, Odisha and West Bengal [, , , , , , , , , , ]. Five studies were conducted in Western India which includes the states like Goa, Gujarat and Maharastra [, , , , ], Ten studies were from Northern India [, , , , , , , , , ], seven studies were from Southern India [, , , , , , ], six studies were from North-East states and two studies were from Central India. Study Settings wise and of the forty studies, twenty-six studies (60%) were conducted in rural areas [, , , , , , –, –, –, , , , –], ten studies were conducted in urban areas (25%)and only six studies (15%) were conducted in tribal areas [, , –, ]. Gender-wise, more than half of the studies (57.5%) were undertaken exclusively on adolescent girls in the age group of 10 to 19 years and two studies (5%) were conducted on only male adolescents [, ]. Eighteen (45%) out of the total forty selected studies were conducted only on school-going adolescents [, , , , , , , , , , , , –, , ]. Summary of included studies indicating the prevalence of stunting and underweight among adolescents in India (between September 2000 and October 2021)

Regarding the prevalence of undernutrition among Indian adolescents, the highest prevalence of stunting was reported in Western India (67.1%) [], and the lowest prevalence was reported in Northern India (12.8%) []. Similarly, the highest prevalence of underweight was reported in Central India (69.0%) [] and the lowest was in Northern India (2.7%) [].

Using the Newcastle–Ottawa Quality Assessment Scale (NOS), All selected studies were evaluated to assess the quality of the studies. Ten studies were found to have a moderate risk of bias or moderate quality which scored 6 to 8, and the rest of the studies had a low risk of bias or high quality. The evaluation of studies was done based on three parameters: i) methodological quality; ii) the comparability of studies; and iii) the outcome measures and data analysis. Adequate sample size calculation and sample selection procedure were not provided by many of the studies. Also, details of the response rate were not defined in the majority of the studies. Very few studies clearly defined and described the statistical test used to analyze data. The measurement of the association was not presented including confidence intervals and the probability level.

The existence of undernutrition among adolescents was primarily reported in two forms such as stunting and underweight. So, we undertook a meta-analysis in these two contexts for a better explanation of the findings.

Nineteen studies reported the prevalence of stunting among Indian adolescents. The pooled prevalence of stunting across nineteen studies was observed as 41.1% (95% Confidence Interval/CI: 35.9 to 46%, I2= 98.6%). The reported prevalence of stunting among 37,830 adolescents ranged from 12.8%—67.1% across the studies. However, there was high heterogeneity among the included studies as observed in the random-effect model analysis.

We investigated whether the year of publication, age, gender, place of study and region had distinct results for our two outcome variables such as stunting and underweight. In the subgroup analysis of all the selected subgroups, the heterogeneity was observed to be high (Fig. 2). Additionally, the pooled prevalence of stunting was observed to be higher among late adolescents (50.8%, 95% CI: 45.8—55.9) than the early adolescents (40.4%, 95% CI: 32.6—48.3) (Fig. 3). Considering study settings, the pooled prevalence of stunting was found higher in tribal areas (46.1%, 95% CI: 22.3- 69.8) followed by rural areas (38.8%, 95% CI: 30.2- 47.5) (Fig. 4). Region-wise, the pooled prevalence estimated for stunting among adolescents was high in Western India (57.6%, 95% CI: 39.2—75.9) followed by North-East (42.0, 95% CI: 29.6 to 54.3) and East India (37.9%, 95% CI: 27.4—48.4) respectively (Fig. 5). The presence of publication bias was assessed through the funnel plot for visual asymmetry, and it was revealed that there was publication bias among the included studies reporting the prevalence of stunting among adolescents in India (Additional file 4, Fig. 1). Leave-One-Out analysis and cumulative meta-analysis of stunting identified that no studies individually influenced the overall results of stunting (Additional file 4, Fig. 2, 3).

Thirty-eight studies were included to estimate the pooled prevalence of adolescents underweight in India. Individual studies reported prevalence of underweight among adolescents ranged from 2.7% to 69.0%. In the random-effects model, the pooled prevalence of underweight among 65,547 adolescents in India from thirty-eight studies was 32.6% with a high heterogeneity.

Subsequently, subgroup analysis was performed based on year of publication, age, gender, place of study, and region. It was observed that the prevalence of underweight among adolescents was higher in the studies published between the years 2005 and 2015 (37.9%, 95% CI: 27.8 – 48.0) compared to those published between 2016 and 2021 (31.2%, 95% CI: 24.4 – 37.9) (Fig. 2). Age-wise subgroup analysis depicted early adolescents (35.2%, 95% CI: 28.2—42.2) as more underweight than late adolescents (29.4%, 95% CI: 23.8—35.0) (Fig. 3). The analysis from the studies conducted in rural, urban and tribal areas revealed that the estimated underweight prevalence rate was high among tribal adolescents (44.9%, 95% CI: 28.3—61.5) followed by rural adolescents (30.9%, 95% CI: 23.3—38.5) (Fig. 4). Subgroup analysis based on region showed that the prevalence of underweight among adolescents was high in Central India (56.6%, 95% CI: 30.9—81.2) followed by the South (37.4%, 95% CI: 23.4—51.4) and North-East India (33.7%, 95% CI: 17.8—49.6) (Fig. 5). The subgroup analysis by gender revealed that the pooled prevalence of underweight among male adolescents was higher (37.8%, 95% CI: 26.3—49.3) than female adolescents (33.1%, 95% CI: 28.4—37.9) (Fig. 6). The results of the subgroup analysis reporting the pooled prevalence of underweight among adolescents by age, gender, year of publication, place of study and region didn’t significantly alter the heterogeneity in this review.

To determine publication bias, a funnel plot and Egger’s statistical test were performed to show bias graphically. The Funnel plot was asymmetrical and Egger’s test result indicated that there was publication bias found among the included studies (Additional file 4, Fig. 4). Leave-one-out and cumulative meta-analysis revealed that none of the studies significantly influenced the overall results (Additional file 4, Fig. 5, 6).

In this systematic review, the selected studies were found of lacking in reporting adequate data. So, the effect of the risk factors or determinants of undernutrition could not be calculated. Similarly, meta-regression of the selected factors could also not be undertaken. We assessed the association of undernutrition with the information on the compared category.

In this systematic review, out of nineteen studies, thirteen studies were included for the analysis of determinants of stunting among adolescents in India [, , , , , , , , , , , , ]. Seven associated factors or determinants of stunting were selected for this analysis. Age, gender, income, family size, caste, education level of parents (father and mother), and parental occupation are the primary determinants of stunting among adolescents in India (Table 3). Similarly, out of thirty-eight studies, twenty-four studies explained the associated factors of underweight among adolescents in India [, , , –, –, , , , –, –, , ]. Age, gender, income, family size, caste, education level of father and mother, and occupation of father and mother were the key risk factors or determinants for adolescents underweight in India which were frequently examined in the included studies. Besides, other associated factors were a vegetarian diet, frequency of meals less than three times/day, birth order, having more than two siblings, and physical activity (Table 4). In stunting, a total of ten studies explored the association between age and stunting among adolescents [, , , , , , , , , ]. In six studies, there was a positive relationship among late adolescents [, , , , , ], while in four studies, there was a negative relationship [, , , ]. It was found in a study that stunting was higher among late adolescents (15–19 years) than early adolescents (10–14 years) and this study also mentioned that in the case of late-adolescent girls, it was more severe []. However, these studies did not explain the underlying differences in age with stunting. In case of factors associated with the prevalence of underweight among adolescents, out of twenty-four included studies, twenty-one studies examined the association between age and underweight among adolescents in India [, , , , , , , , , , , –, , –, , ]. Of them, fifteen studies reported that there was a significant association between early adolescence and underweight [, , , , , , , , , –, , , ]. It indicates that a high prevalence of underweight was observed in early adolescence possibly due to the increased physiologic growth associated nutritional requirement and non-availability of adequate food and other comorbidities. However, six studies showed a negative association between early adolescence and being underweight [, , , , , ].

Regarding the relationship between gender and the prevalence of adolescent stunting in India, among six studies [, , , , , ], four studies reported a positive relationship between adolescent girls and stunting [, , , ]. Pal et al. [] found that poor diet and disease are the immediate underlying factors of stunting among adolescent girls in India []. In relation to gender with underweight, eight studies assessed the association between gender and underweight [, , , , , , , ]. Apart from one study, adolescent boys were more likely to be underweight in all seven studies []. Bhattacharya et al. (2021) emphasized that boys in comparison to girls were more prone to suffer from being underweight as they spent more time playing outdoors with high exposure to dirty environments and poor hygienic practices []. We did not find any report describing the effect of son preference leading to undernourishment for the girl child in the families.

The association between the income of the family and the prevalence of undernourishment, particularly in the context of stunting, was shown as a major risk factor in most of the selected studies. Particularly adolescents from low-income families are at higher risk of stunting compared to adolescents from families of other income groups. Among eight studies [, , , , , , , ], seven reported a positive relationship between low income and adolescent stunting in India. Only one study showed a negative association between stunting and the low income of the families []. As noted above, Kumar et al.(2021) reported that poverty played a major role in poor growth and nutritional deficiency among adolescents []. For underweight, thirteen studies examined the relationship between family income and underweight among adolescents [, , , , , , , , , , , , ]. There were eight studies [, , , , , , , ] that reported a positive association between low family income and adolescent underweight and five studies mentioned that there was no significant association between family income and underweight among adolescents [, , , , ]. So, in this above context, we have listed the studies (Table 3) and their findings regarding association of family income and undernutrition.

The educational qualification of parents influences the nutritional status, dietary pattern, and access to better healthcare facilities for children. Six studies reported the association between parental education [, , , , , ] and the prevalence of stunting among adolescent children; there were four studies that exclusively focused on the association between maternal education and adolescent stunting [, , , ], two reported a positive association between maternal education and adolescent stunting [, ]. Factors like mothers with higher education due to their exposure to the outside world, better understanding of healthcare and nutritional care of their families were major determinants []. Education empowers women to make independent decisions and greater access to household resources which are important for improving the nutritional status of the members of the families []. Regarding the association between paternal education and the prevalence of stunting among adolescents, four studies out of five showed no significant association between lower paternal education and stunting among adolescents in India [, , , ]. Regarding underweight, thirteen studies were assessed the association between the educational background of parents and the prevalence of underweight [, , , , , , , , , , , , ]. Among those, in five studies, there was a significant relationship between low paternal education (primary education or illiterate) and adolescent underweight [, , , , ]. In relation to maternal education also, this scenario was the same. There was a positive association between low maternal education and adolescent underweight prevalence as examined in seven studies [, , , , , , ]. Low parental education increases the risk of being underweight or thin. As pointed out by Chandrashekarappa et al. [], parental education plays an important role in providing adequate and nutritious food to their children [].

A total of five studies investigated the association between father’s occupation with the prevalence of stunting among adolescents [, , , , ]. Among those, three studies found a positive association between paternal occupations who were as daily wage labourers and the prevalence of stunting among adolescents [, , ]. However, where the male parent had jobs or businesses, the child was observed to have less chance of stunting. However, the findings on female parents’ working status showed a reverse trend. Two studies reported a positive relationship between working mothers and the prevalence of stunting among adolescents [, ]. With respect to the mother’s working status, adolescents of non-working mothers were less likely to be stunted compared to working mothers []. Concerning the underweight prevalence, four studies reported and described a positive association between working mothers and underweight prevalence among adolescents [, , , ]. Likewise, seven studies showed a positive relationship between paternal occupation (particularly daily wage labourers or unemployed) with the occurrence of underweight among adolescents [, , , , , , , ].

Family size is a crucial factor in low- and middle-income households in defining access to an adequate amount of food for all children. In the present analysis, we found only two studies examining the relationship between the prevalence of adolescent stunting and family size [, ]. Both studies reported that the smaller the family size, the higher the prevalence of stunting rate. Adolescents in joint families were found less likely to be stunted than those in nuclear families []. Similarly, with regard to the association between family size and underweight, the analysis gave a mixed result [, , , , , , ]. Three studies reported children from joint families were more susceptible to being underweight [, , ]. The findings are contrary to other findings that reported an increase in family size has a greater impact on the family expenditure on health matters and also less access to a healthy nutritional diet which is more likely to be underweight []. In joint families particularly, due to intra-household distribution of food, the family members were less likely to get adequate protein and vitamin-rich food [].

Caste is a typical characteristic of the Indian social system defining the distribution of power, association, and access as well as a reason for disparities in various forms. Particularly, families of disadvantaged or marginalized castes/groups face difficulties in getting adequate food all over India. In the present study, we found six studies where the role of caste has been examined in defining the nutritional status of adolescent children [, , , , , ]. In only one study [], the relationship between caste and stunting prevalence was evaluated where it reported that the prevalence of stunting was higher among adolescents from the disadvantaged caste/groups, particularly among the Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe (SC/ST). In case of underweight prevalence, caste was also examined in six studies [, , , , , ]. Among these six studies, four reported a positive association between disadvantaged caste and the prevalence of underweight [, , , ], whereas two studies showed no relationship [, ]. The high risk of occurrence of underweight was more among the disadvantaged caste population compared to the middle or higher caste possible due to their non-affordability, inaccessibility, and unavailability of health care services and nutritional diet [].

sections.title: Discussion
sections.text:
The findings of this systematic review revealed that at least one in every two adolescents is suffering from stunting (19 studies; 41.1% pooled prevalence; 95% CI: 35.9, 46.0), while one in every three adolescents is underweight (38 studies; 32.6% pooled prevalence; 95% CI: 26.8, 37.1). However, there was substantial heterogeneity in meta-analysis estimates; the small number of studies and wide variation in sample and study characteristics existed around the pooled risk estimates. The present findings around adolescent stunting show a concerning state which is higher than even low-income countries like Ethiopia 20–30% [, , ],. Similarly, the prevalence of underweight was also observed in a similar pattern where it is higher compared to several South Asian countries like Bangladesh, Myanmar and Pakistan (21%) [, ]. However, it may be mentioned here that there is a major fall in prevalence of undernutrition in last 10 years than the previous decade while the major burden of this disadvantage situation still lies with tribal population section.

Here it can be mentioned that several nutrition and food-related supplementation programs like the Mid-day meal program, Poshan Abhiyan, and National Nutritional Anemia Prophylaxis Programme are being undertaken under the national nutrition policy. For real-time monitoring of nutritional outcomes, the government of India developed the Poshan tracker app in 2021. Despite lots of intervention strategies adopted by the government of India, the expected control was less observed from the studies and the prevalence of undernutrition is still high in India. So, it signifies thorough evaluation and radical changes in the strategizing process are highly necessary. It further highlights that a holistic intervention rather than simple food supplementation may hold the key where issues like socio-economic inequality, the disparity in various socio-cultural aspects, illiteracy, women empowerment, lack of affordability, heavy indebtedness among poor, unavailability, along with inaccessibility to proper nutritional diet and healthcare services are addressed in a time-bound manner. In-depth research around food behaviour, dietary practices, standard of food being consumed on daily basis, effect of food price inflation on household consumption etc. is the need of the hour.

There were nine major associated factors found in the included studies relating to stunting and underweight prevalence among adolescents in India. Inadequate access to necessary diet during the growth phase (such as adolescence) was found as a major risk factor in the studies. Particularly late adolescent age groups (15–19 years) were observed to be more at risk of being stunted compared to early adolescents age group (10 to 14 years). On the contrary, the prevalence of underweight was higher among early adolescents; similar findings were recently reported in a systematic review conducted in Ethiopia []. The risk of being underweight was higher among male children compared to female adolescents. This result is in line with the situations as reported in other South Asian countries []. This variation might be associated with differences in physical activity between male and female adolescents. Male adolescents are more physically active than their female counterparts []. Though son preference, a typical cultural practice in Indian patriarchal society and plays a crucial role in the distribution of nutritious food in the family, the findings did not suggest any such effect in the selected studies. Similarly, the socio-economic status or income of the family is one of the significant determinants contributing to the prevalence of stunting and underweight among adolescents in India. The findings also confirmed that the prevalence of stunting and underweight are more concentrated among adolescents belonging to low-income families similar to previous work conducted in Sri Lanka [] and Bangladesh []. Low family income heavily limits the nutritious dietary pattern and frequency of meals of the family members, particularly the children and adolescents which have a relative impact on the physical growth and mental development of adolescents. Higher income of family leads to higher availability of food and associated resources which ultimately supports the nutritional status of the family members [].

Parental educational status was also found as an important associated factor for stunting and underweight prevalence among adolescents similar to the findings in the studies conducted in South Asia [, , ]. Educated parents are more vigilant on children’s nutritional and healthcare requirements. It might be possibly associated with higher nutritional awareness as well as better healthcare practices. Particularly, adolescents with educated mothers have lower chances of being undernourished [, , ]. However, this review also revealed that children of working mothers tended to show a higher prevalence of undernutrition than housewives which indicates possible heavy workplace burden leading to children’s insufficient and improper feeding.

The association between family size with the prevalence of adolescent stunting and underweight was reported in the selected studies. Adolescents living within nuclear families were more likely to suffer from undernutrition. This finding was contrary to the findings reported in other countries [, –]. This review also revealed that children from disadvantaged castes particularly scheduled caste and scheduled tribes were at higher risk of stunting and being underweight in India []. In the nutritional domain, adolescents from disadvantaged caste are significantly lower in health aspects. Also, caste-based discrimination prohibits the disadvantaged caste people from accessing government healthcare services and other nutrition-related facilities [, ]. It is in line with the findings of Bogin (2021) where he argued that the complex interplay of societal, political and economic factors influences growth patterns, health disparities, and well-being [].

The present systematic review brings in the detailed prevalence and pattern of undernutrition among the adolescent population in India for the first time and highlights a comprehensive detail of associated influencing factors. The review indicates that Indian adolescents are in the most vulnerable state to undernutrition which is a major public health challenge for the country []. Dietary patterns and physical activity, socioeconomic conditions, in addition to lack of access to schooling (drop-outs), various disparities, and prevailing social practices and cultural norms like early marriage, and caste discrimination were observed to influence the health and nutritional well-being of adolescents. Here, it needs to be highlighted that undernutrition has numerous long-term consequences such as poor physical and mental function, increased vulnerability to infections, development of non-communicable diseases in adulthood, and economic burden on the healthcare system [, ]. So, the present study highlights the urgent need to consider the potential implications of adolescent undernutrition for policy and practice. This review will help healthcare practitioners and policymakers to evaluate the ongoing intervention strategies as well as identifying the gaps and challenges. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first systematic review revealing the prevalence of undernutrition among adolescents in India.

The findings from the present review identified several knowledge gaps at overall level as well as in the studies on the prevalence of undernutrition among adolescents in India that should be addressed in future research. First, all the available literature were cross-sectional and quantitative studies, which highlights the major gap in understanding and evidence around pathways of acquiring stunting/underweight and the process of influence of associated factors. This designates a need for longitudinal studies with qualitative aspects and including other research methods (including molecular, biological, microbial etc.) to identify possible risk factors of undernutrition. Second, this systematic review also identified that there is a large-scale paucity of evidence in India, for example, Central and Western parts of India largely lack prevalence reporting on stunting; most of the studies on stunting were conducted in Eastern India. Also, it indicated that research on the prevalence of adolescent stunting was very less compared to underweight prevalence research. Furthermore, with methodological bias, only nineteen studies used stunting as a parameter to measure undernutrition, though both stunting and underweight should be measured to determine the prevalence of undernutrition. Third, evidence reporting the community characteristics, and community-specific literature on undernutrition among vulnerable populations and settings like slums, tribal areas, refugee settings, internally displaced settings as well as among drop-outs could not be identified for this review, as there is a paucity of literature on those communities. Fourth, the included studies largely focused on the female population. Hence, the pooled estimates were not generalizable to males. Fifth, most of the literature identified age, gender, income, parental education, and occupation as the major and common associated factors of adolescent undernutrition, however, they could not be measured through meta-regression due to lack of sufficient and detailed data. Stunting defined as low height-for-age, is often used as an indicator of chronic undernutrition. However, the relationship between stunting and malnutrition is not straightforward, it is important to recognise that stunting does not always equate to malnutrition []. Stunting, underweight, and other growth indicators are often used as proxies for malnutrition, but relying solely on these measures can be misleading []. Though these indicators reflect overall growth patterns, they do not directly assess whether a child or adolescent is experiencing nutritional deficiencies. To accurately identify malnutrition, direct empirical measurements of nutritional deficiencies are essential. Research should also cover other related factors like dietary patterns, physical activity, hygiene, and sanitation []. Besides these, several other factors, beyond inadequate dietary intake, infections and disease burden, environmental conditions and psychosocial factors can contribute to compromised growth which needs to be investigated [–]. However, majority of the studies in the present review have adopted a view similar to WHO definition of stunting. The data on the nutritional status of slums and tribal adolescents as well as dropouts and associated factors are lacking in national-level surveys like the National Family Health Survey [, ]; Comprehensive National Nutrition Survey (CNNS), 2019 explored only some of the socio-economic factors.

Besides the gaps in the availability of evidence, there are limitations in the inclusion of various factors in the evidence. For example, the study found marked heterogeneity observed across the included studies indicating substantial differences in the prevalence of adolescent undernutrition across various regions of India. This is due to the variations in study design, differences in measurement tools and criteria, socio-economic diversity, and the uneven geographic distribution of studies. Many Indian states reported with not a single study report on the undernutrition status of adolescents; it indicates more studies are needed to be executed to reflect better representation of the Indian adolescents. Due to the uneven distribution of studies across geographic regions, the pooled prevalence estimates might not fully capture the variations in stunting across different contexts within India. Regions with limited data might exhibit different risk factors and prevalence rates, which remain underexplored. Expanding research coverage would provide a more accurate and equitable understanding of adolescent undernutrition in India. Though study characteristics like places of study, region, age, gender, and years of publications depicted the prevalence of undernutrition among adolescents, there was a lack of detailed reporting of individual-level characteristics like schooling status and some other associated factors like parental education, caste, low socio-economic status, the family size etc. in many studies. The study has utilized only the electronically available studies and also those studies published in the English language only.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.text: The present analysis is in line with the recent observation by the Department of Biotechnology, Govt. of India [, ]. Though there is a significant improvement in adolescent nutritional status in India in last 10 years, the long standing burden of stunting and underweight among adolescents is still high. The present review indicates the need for strategic improvement in undernutrition research, intervention and scaling-up strategy. Additionally, it is time to understand stunting as a result of multiple and complex adversities that simply explain as undernutrition. Possibly, an integrative approach of nutritional strategies associated with effective healthcare facilities and socio-economic upliftment can help reduce such prevalence of undernutrition among Indian adolescents. Further, it is highly important to identify the emerging research priorities in this field which has not yet been understood or studied. Research studies, particularly, targeting deprived sections with a biosocial and behavioural prioritisation may hold the key. Extension of food supplementation to adolescents through various schemes like mid-day meals may be extended beyond the present age group (i.e. up to 14 years) and up to college level may bring substantial outcome in addressing adolescent undernutrition.
